item.title: Multi-modal Laplace-based sampling
item.description: arXiv:2611.03773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the multi-modal Laplace approximation, given by a weighted Gaussian mixture centred at the local minima of the negative log-density, for sampling from probability measures that concentrate around finitely many modes as an inverse-temperature parameter $n$ grows. Such distributions occur in Bayesian inference in the small noise or large data regime. We derive explicit, non-asymptotic bounds on the Hellinger distance between the multi-modal Laplace approximation and the concentrating posterior. The bound decays like $n^{-1/2}$ with $n$ and the constants depend only polynomially on the dimension $d$. Moreover, we analyse the Laplace mixture as a proposal distribution for self-normalised importance sampling and independent Metropolis--Hastings (IMH) targeting concentration multimodal distributions. We derive asymptotic results, as $n\to\infty$, on the effective sample size in case of importance sampling as well as on the average acceptance probability, lag-one autocorrelation, and spectral gap in case of IMH. Numerical experiments illustrate and verify our theoretical findings.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Eg\'ea, Hanyue Gu, Daniel Rudolf, Bj\"orn Sprungk

item.title: A Tetration Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2611.03895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a one-parameter family of continuous distributions on the unit interval whose cumulative distribution functions are given by the odd-height power towers \(x\uparrow\uparrow n\) (\(n=1,3,5,\dots\)). The associated densities admit a simple recursive formula obtained by logarithmic differentiation. We prove that every such density is strictly positive on \((0,1)\) and integrates to one, thereby establishing that the construction yields a genuine probability distribution. Numerical investigation reveals a characteristic peak--dip--rise shape: a sharp mode lying just below \(e^{-e}\) for all examined heights, followed by a trough and a gradual recovery toward density value~1 at the right endpoint. We then identify the limiting distribution as the height tends to infinity through odd integers.
item.dc:creator: Micah Thornton

item.title: Minimax signal detection in regression under differential privacy
item.description: arXiv:2611.04064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish minimax separation rates across sparsity levels for regression signal detection under $(\epsilon, \delta)$-central differential privacy, considering linear regression with an unknown error distribution and generalised linear models (GLMs) with an unknown intercept. Without sparsity restrictions, the separation rates for linear regression and GLMs with binary responses match the private Gaussian mean testing rate up to polylogarithmic factors. For GLMs with more than two possible response outcomes, additional information in the marginal response distribution permits faster detection of sufficiently small signals when the dimension exceeds the sample size $n$. Our upper bounds are based on a reduction to private mean testing, tests of dependence between the response and sparse covariate projections, and a response-only test that is adjusted for the unknown intercept. The resulting procedure adapts to unknown sparsity and matches our lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. We also construct polynomial-time tests that attain these rates when $\epsilon\gtrsim n^{-1/2}$, and compare their numerical performance with existing private procedures.
item.dc:creator: Elly K. H. Hung

item.title: A Bayesian-Geometric Reading of Classical Model-Based Optimal Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.04450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical model-based optimal design criteria (D-, T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality) are usually motivated via the Cram\'er--Rao bound as optimizing scalar functions of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). This paper offers a complementary reading in which each criterion appears asymptotically as $N \to \infty$ as the leading-order term of an expected dissimilarity between prior and posterior, with the FIM entering through the Bernstein--von Mises limit. The Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of the posterior relative to the prior recovers D-optimality (classically known); a reverse KL of the prior relative to the posterior recovers T-optimality (here defined as maximization of the trace of the FIM, following one common convention) and its weighted-trace generalization; and a first-order approximation of the squared 2-Wasserstein distance recovers L-, C- and A-optimality. The five criteria emerge as instances of a common Bayesian-geometric template, indexed by three choices: the dissimilarity, the prior parametrization, and the approximation scheme used to evaluate it (e.g.\ Taylor expansions of the matrix square root). For the weighted criteria, the Gaussian prior covariance encodes the criterion's weight matrix, so any choice of weights corresponds to a specific prior in the family. The T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality derivations appear novel to the best of my knowledge. A sixth criterion, E-optimality, is recovered not as an independent expected-dissimilarity limit but as a min-max robustification of C-optimality against uncertainty in the modeler's prior direction. The framework is extended to distinguish between a designer's prior over unknown parameters at design time and a modeler's prior used for posterior inference, recovering the classical expected information gain objective as a special case.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Tarek

item.title: Nuisance structure and the detection boundary for population size: how profiling can change a rate, not only a constant
item.description: arXiv:2611.04453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A system contains an unknown number $N$ of units, each failing at an unknown common rate, each unit is removed once it fails. The failure-rate declines as units are removed, but after only a few failures the decline is too slight to distinguish from a constant rate, and the maximum-likelihood estimate of $N$ is infinite with substantial probability. This is a well-known feature of the model, but its probability has not been quantified. We show that about $N^{2/3}$ failures are needed before a finite population can be distinguished from an inexhaustible one, and that at this scale the profile log-likelihood ratio converges to that of a Gaussian shift experiment, in which an infinite estimate occurs with a calculable probability. The exponent is not a property of the model alone. Profiling annihilates the Taylor terms that the nuisance-parameters can reproduce, and detectability is governed by the first surviving term. For example, unknown drift in testing-effort reproduces the linear term, leaving a quadratic survivor and raising the requirement to $N^{4/5}$; in general the critical scale is $N^{2q/(2q+1)}$ for a survivor of order $q$. We obtain the limiting-law of the estimator, the null likelihood ratio distribution, and confidence sets that may be unbounded.
item.dc:creator: Yakir Berchenko

item.title: Estimating "Realized" Skewness using Convolutional Neural Network
item.description: arXiv:2611.04598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a new estimator of low-frequency skewness (monthly) that exploits high-frequency data (5 min) through a direct functional mapping consisting of layers of Convolutional Neural Networks followed by Multi Layer Perceptrons. Monte Carlo experiments involving stochastic volatility models, with and without jumps, show that the estimator reduces finite-sample bias relative to existing realized-skewness estimators and remains accurate under model misspecification. Empirically, our estimator exhibits temporal stability and delivers cross-sectional performance in actual skewness-sorted portfolios. We characterize the finite-sample bias of conventional plug-in skewness estimators and establish risk consistency properties of the proposed NN estimator under standard regularity conditions.
item.dc:creator: Haozhe Jiang, Ostap Okhrin, Michael Rockinger

item.title: Approximating Distributions on Vertex Degrees in Random Hypergraphs via Stein's Method
item.description: arXiv:2611.04705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex data are increasingly represented as hypergraphs. We establish bounds for approximating joint vertex-degree distributions by independent multivariate Poisson and correlated normal distributions in hypergraph models with independent hyperedges. We discuss the approximation of the distribution under different density regimes which are further supported by simulation studies.
item.dc:creator: Xianghe Zhu, Wenkai Xu, Gesine Reinert

item.title: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity
item.description: arXiv:2611.05277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but exchangeability can fail when deployment changes the data distribution. We study conformal prediction in performative settings, where the deployed predictor affects the data distribution, and seek prediction sets valid at performative equilibrium: coverage must hold under $D(f^\star)$ for a performatively stable predictor $f^\star$. Under total-variation $L$-sensitivity of the distribution map, we prove a phase transition at $L=1$. If $L \ge 1$, no finite-sample procedure can uniformly guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial prediction sets. If $L<1$, the minimax excess miscoverage over informative procedures is $\widetilde{\Omega}(1/((1-L)\sqrt{n}))$, implying a sample-complexity inflation of order $1/(1-L)^2$ for fixed excess miscoverage. Our main technical tool is a transfer theorem: any procedure returning a predictor within $\varepsilon$ of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive $L\varepsilon$ term after split-conformal calibration. We instantiate the theorem with two retraining algorithms: a model-free method for discretizable classes and a parametric tail-averaged method that matches the $n$- and $L$-dependence of this rate up to logarithmic factors. Experiments, including semi-synthetic credit scoring, demonstrate the predicted threshold behavior and scaling laws.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Mahrous, Roberto Di Pietro

item.title: Logit-based alternatives to two-stage least squares
item.description: arXiv:2312.10333v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose logit-based IV and augmented logit-based IV estimators that serve as alternatives to the traditionally used 2SLS estimator in the model where both the endogenous treatment variable and the corresponding instrument are binary. Our novel estimators are as easy to compute as the 2SLS estimator but have an advantage over the 2SLS estimator in terms of causal interpretability. In particular, in certain cases where the probability limits of both our estimators and the 2SLS estimator take the form of weighted-average treatment effects, our estimators are guaranteed to yield non-negative weights whereas the 2SLS estimator is not.
item.dc:creator: Denis Chetverikov, Jinyong Hahn, Zhipeng Liao, Shuyang Sheng

item.title: Bayesian Filters via the Stochastic Category
item.description: arXiv:2611.03830v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We extend the categorical treatment of Bayesian filters to models with feedback, whose transitions and observations may depend on the past observations. We work in the stochastic category, whose objects are measurable spaces and whose morphisms are Markov kernels, which we refer to as stochastic morphisms. We systematically parameterize stochastic morphisms by a measurable space, and develop the calculus of conditioning in a notation intuitively compatible with classical probability theory, requiring neither string diagrams nor densities. A stochastic morphism into a product space is regarded as a parameterized family of joint laws, and its conditional law is again a stochastic morphism, so that the rules of conditioning become equalities of stochastic morphisms. We define the Bayesian inverse with respect to a parameterized prior and prove Bayesian coherence. A model with feedback is then a model whose parameter space grows with the observations, and we derive the Bayesian filter, prediction and smoothing for such models, with standard Borel hidden states and countably generated observation spaces. The affine Gaussian stochastic morphisms parameterized by a measurable space form a family strictly larger than the Markov category $\mathbf{Gauss}$, closed under composition and Bayesian inversion, in which we obtain the Kalman filter and the Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother with feedback.
item.dc:creator: Kenichi Bannai, Masahiro Kurisaki

item.title: StreamLTT: Risk Certification for Policy Selection under Stream Dependence
item.description: arXiv:2611.04062v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learn-then-Test (LTT) provides a general framework for certifying deployment policies against a prescribed risk target, but its standard formulation targets a fixed population risk estimated from calibration losses. In sequential deployment, losses may instead be dependent and nonstationary, so the risk of a fixed policy can evolve with the observed history. We introduce StreamLTT, which replaces this fixed population risk with average predictable risk, defined by conditioning each decision's loss on the information available before its outcome is revealed. Conditional centering turns empirical deviations from this target into a martingale sum, enabling both a test that adapts to predictable variance and a finite-sample Hoeffding alternative. Combined with family-wise error rate control, StreamLTT yields a simultaneously certified policy region that supports subsequent deployment selection. Across seven forecasting datasets and seven deployment risks, StreamLTT places the certified frontier substantially closer to the prescribed risk target than IID, robust-variance, block-bootstrap, and concentration-based alternatives, while empirical family-wise error closely follows the prescribed level. A finite-sample ablation further shows that the predictable-risk formulation drives the tighter risk frontier, while adaptation to predictable variance makes more effective use of the available family-wise error budget. StreamLTT therefore extends risk-certified policy selection to dependent deployment streams by addressing both what risk should be certified and how it should be tested.
item.dc:creator: Jinwen Xu, Qin Lu

item.title: Nonparametric GARCH: An Iterated Neural Estimator
item.description: arXiv:2611.04157v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study nonparametric estimation and forecasting for GARCH-type processes and propose an iterated neural estimator that alternates between estimating the recursion map and updating the unobserved conditional variances. Under mild conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for the time-averaged in-sample variance-path error and show that the estimator is minimax rate-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Under stationarity and mixing conditions, we establish the same rate for recursion-map estimation and derive finite-sample bounds for out-of-sample variance forecasts and expected excess Gaussian quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss. The convergence rates depend on the true lag orders and remain unchanged when the fitted orders are overspecified. Simulation studies illustrate the effectiveness of our estimators under nonlinear and time-varying volatility dynamics. Real-data applications suggest that our neural methods perform competitively and can incorporate option-price and high-frequency information.
item.dc:creator: Ruizhi Deng, Guohao Shen, Ngai Hang Chan

item.title: Inferential Issues in Model-based Small Area Estimation: Some History and Selective Recent Advances
item.description: arXiv:2611.04281v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model-based Small Area Estimation (SAE) has seen rapid growth over the past 25 years or so due to the rapidly increasing demand for reliable small area estimators of totals, means and more complex area parameters. Direct area-specific estimators are either unreliable (due to small area-specific sample sizes) or not feasible (due to zero area-specific sample sizes). It is therefore necessary to borrow strength from related areas through implicit or explicit models linking related areas. We focus on explicit area-level and unit-level models. After a brief historical sketch of the evolution of SAE, we focus on selective recent developments (mostly after 2015). Developments before 2015 are mostly covered in the comprehensive Wiley book by Rao and Molina (2015). Under a basic area-level model, we consider semi-parametric and robust estimation of small area means under model misspecifications. Under a basic unit level model, methods for estimating complex parameters, such as poverty indicators, will be presented, including robust estimation in the presence of outliers. A comparison of area-level and unit-level models when unit level data are available will also be presented. Estimation methods studied include empirical best linear unbiased prediction (EBLUP), empirical best (EB) and hierarchical Bayes (HB).
item.dc:creator: J. N. K. Rao, J. Sunil Rao

item.title: Decentralized Sparse Quantile Regression
item.description: arXiv:2611.04612v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distributed statistical learning has recently attracted significant attention owing to its computational efficiency and scalability in large-scale systems. However, the non-smooth quantile loss poses substantial challenges to the development of efficient decentralized algorithms for quantile regression. Existing methods may either suffer from slow convergence or rely on smoothing-based approximations that require additional stringent assumptions, particularly in high-dimensional settings. To address these issues, we propose a decentralized framework that integrates gradient tracking with iterative hard thresholding for sparse quantile estimation. The proposed method avoids smoothing approximations and relaxes the initialization requirement. Theoretically, we show that the proposed algorithm achieves linear convergence under stated regularity conditions and that the resulting estimator attains the same order of statistical accuracy as its centralized counterpart. We further develop a decentralized information criterion for selecting the working sparsity level and establish support screening guarantees. Numerical experiments and a real-data study illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Changxin Yang, Jianwei Shi, Zhongyi Zhu

item.title: On the Onsager--Machlup functional of the infinite-dimensional angular central Gaussian distribution and related measures
item.description: arXiv:2611.04781v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Onsager--Machlup functional of a probability measure is a generalisation of the negative logarithm of the probability density function, defined precisely using the ratios of masses of balls in the limit of vanishing radius. It plays an important role in several areas of applied mathematics because its minimisers can be understood as modes of the measure. We show that the Onsager--Machlup functional of the angular central Gaussian measure on the unit sphere of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space---i.e., the radial projection of a centred Gaussian measure with covariance operator $C$---is constant on the finite-dimensional sphere spanned by the eigenvectors of leading eigenvalue under $C$, and takes the value $+\infty$ elsewhere. We discuss the consequences of this extreme concentration of mass for maximum a posteriori estimation in Bayesian inverse problems with an angular central Gaussian prior.
item.dc:creator: Hefin Lambley, T. J. Sullivan, Sam Taylor

item.title: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs
item.description: arXiv:2611.05114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give an algorithm for PAC learning intersections of $k$ degree-2 polynomial threshold functions over $R^d$ under a Gaussian distribution. Our algorithm achieves classification error $\epsilon$ using $d^{O(k)}2^{O_k(\log^3(1/\epsilon))}$ time and samples, improving over the $d^{O(k^2/\epsilon^2)}$ running time of the polynomial regression approach. To our knowledge, our result is the first to obtain a dimension exponent independent of the accuracy parameter, even for $k=2$. We complement our algorithmic result with an SQ lower bound showing that the complexity dependence of $d^{\Omega(k)}$ is unavoidable. Lifting the input to polynomial features turns the target into an intersection of $k$ halfspaces. This suggests using the first two labeled moments for subspace recovery. In the lifted space, however, these moments can reveal nothing. Our starting point is a Gaussian comparison theorem showing that, for sufficiently regular defining quadratics, the labeled moments needed for subspace recovery are approximately preserved. To handle arbitrary defining quadratics, we establish a new structural result showing that every direction with significant resampling influence can be detected through degree-$O(k)$ moments. These results yield an initial $d^{O(k)}2^{\mathrm{poly}_k(1/\epsilon)}$-time learner using adaptive restrictions. To improve the exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$, we develop a two-stage dimension-reduction approach that avoids the costly adaptive partitioning. After identifying a subspace containing all directions with large influence, we use generalized regularity and Gaussian comparison to recover the remaining relevant quadratic features through a new derivative-based moment operator. The recovered features support an intersection close to the target. Combining them with robust hinge-loss minimization gives our quasipolynomial-time learner.
item.dc:creator: Ilias Diakonikolas, Daniel M. Kane, Mingchen Ma, Lisheng Ren, Trung Tran

item.title: Ensembles of Random Partition-Based Models under Covariate Shift
item.description: arXiv:2611.05195v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distribution shifts, including covariate shifts, are ubiquitous in real-world applications of machine learning. Empirical evidence suggests that, across a variety of models with and without downstream adaptation, ensembles tend to be more robust to covariate shift than single models. We extend the theory of covariate shift severity from single models to ensembles, providing theoretical justification for the empirical trends. We introduce new discrepancy measures of covariate shift severity to control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators. We then show that with sufficient ensemble size, these models can achieve minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift. Our results suggest that modelers can expect to need larger ensemble sizes for more severe covariate shifts.
item.dc:creator: Mary Versa Clemens-Sewall, Eliza O'Reilly

item.title: Asymmetric conformal prediction with penalized kernel sum-of-squares
item.description: arXiv:2601.22834v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) is a distribution-free method to construct reliable prediction intervals that has gained significant attention in recent years. Despite its success and various proposed extensions, a significant practical feature which has been overlooked in previous research is the potential skewed nature of the noise, or of the residuals when the predictive model exhibits bias. In this work, we leverage recent developments in CP to propose a new asymmetric procedure that bridges the gap between skewed and non-skewed noise distributions, while still maintaining adaptivity of the prediction intervals. We introduce a new statistical learning problem to construct adaptive and asymmetric prediction bands, with a unique feature based on a penalty which promotes symmetry: when its intensity varies, the intervals smoothly change from symmetric to asymmetric ones. This learning problem is based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and the recently introduced kernel sum-of-squares framework. First, we establish representer theorems to make our problem tractable in practice, and derive dual formulations which are essential for scalability to larger datasets. Second, the intensity of the penalty is chosen using a novel data-driven method which automatically identifies the symmetric nature of the noise. We show that consenting to some asymmetry can let the learned prediction bands better adapt to small sample regimes or biased predictive models.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Forty-Third International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), Jul 2026, S{\'e}oul, South Korea
item.dc:creator: Louis Allain (ENSAI, CREST), S{\'e}bastien Da Veiga (ENSAI, CREST, RT-UQ), Brian Staber

item.title: The Pivotal Information Criterion
item.description: arXiv:2603.04172v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Bayesian and Akaike information criteria aim at finding a good balance between under- and over-fitting. They are extensively used every day by practitioners. Yet we contend they suffer from at least two afflictions: their penalty parameters $\lambda=\log n$ and $\lambda=2$ are too small, leading to many false discoveries, and their inherent (best subset) discrete optimization is infeasible in high dimension. We alleviate these issues with the pivotal information criterion: PIC is defined as a continuous optimization problem, and the PIC penalty parameter $\lambda$ is selected at the detection boundary (under pure noise). PIC's choice of $\lambda$ is an upper quantile of a statistic that we prove to be (asymptotically) pivotal, provided the loss function is appropriately transformed. As a result, simulations show a phase transition in the probability of exact support recovery with PIC, a phenomenon studied with no noise in compressed sensing. Applied to real data, for similar predictive performances, PIC selects the least complex model among state-of-the-art learners.
item.dc:creator: Sylvain Sardy, Maxime van Cutsem, Sara van de Geer

item.title: Statistical and Computational Limits for Cumulant Tensor Inference: A Regime in Which Efficient Detection Is Harder Than Efficient Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2603.26029v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study estimation and detection of high-order cumulant tensors from $n$ i.i.d. observations of a $p$-dimensional random vector, with performance measured in the tensor spectral norm. Under sub-Gaussianity, we show that the minimax rate for estimating the order-$d$ cumulant tensor is $\sqrt{p/n}\wedge 1$. In contrast to covariance estimation, the natural plug-in estimator obtained by replacing population moments in the moment--cumulant formula with sample moments, which we call the sample cumulant tensor, is generally not rate-optimal for $d\ge 3$, and we construct an estimator that attains the minimax rate. On the computational side, we study testing whether the $d$-th order cumulant tensor vanishes after whitening. We provide evidence, under a model-specific low-degree conjecture, that detection is computationally hard when $n\ll p^{d/2}$. At the same time, we identify a regime in which an efficiently computable estimator achieves error smaller than the separation at which polynomial-time tests can reliably distinguish the null from the alternative under the same conjecture. This reveals an unusual reverse detection--estimation gap: computationally efficient detection can be harder than computationally efficient estimation. The underlying reason is that the relevant loss, tensor spectral norm, is itself NP-hard to compute, creating a new form of computational--statistical gap.
item.dc:creator: Runshi Tang, Yuefeng Han, Anru R. Zhang

item.title: Analysis of The Limiting Spectral Distribution of Large Random Matrices of The Mar\v{c}enko-Pastur Type
item.description: arXiv:2408.10068v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Consider the random matrix \(\bW_n = \bB_n + n^{-1}\bX_n^*\bA_n\bX_n\), where \(\bA_n\) and \(\bB_n\) are Hermitian matrices of dimensions \(p \times p\) and \(n \times n\), respectively, and \(\bX_n\) is a \(p \times n\) random matrix with independent and identically distributed entries of mean 0 and variance 1. Assume that \(p\) and \(n\) grow to infinity proportionally, and that the spectral measures of \(\bA_n\) and \(\bB_n\) converge as \(p, n \to \infty\) towards two probability measures \(\calA\) and \(\calB\). Building on the groundbreaking work of \cite{marchenko1967distribution}, which demonstrated that the empirical spectral distribution of \(\bW_n\) converges towards a probability measure \(F\) characterized by its Stieltjes transform, this paper investigates the properties of \(F\) when \(\calB\) is a general measure. We show that \(F\) has an analytic density at the region near where the Stieltjes transform of $\calB$ is bounded. The density closely resembles \(C\sqrt{|x - x_0|}\) near certain edge points \(x_0\) of its support for a wide class of \(\calA\) and \(\calB\). We provide a complete characterization of the support of \(F\). Moreover, we show that \(F\) can exhibit discontinuities at points where \(\calB\) is discontinuous.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Li

item.title: Scalable and adaptive prediction bands with kernel sum-of-squares
item.description: arXiv:2505.21039v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) is a popular framework for constructing prediction bands with valid coverage in finite samples, while being free of any distributional assumption. A well-known limitation of conformal prediction is the lack of adaptivity, although several works introduced practically efficient alternate procedures. In this work, we build upon recent ideas that rely on recasting the CP problem as a statistical learning problem, directly targeting coverage and adaptivity. This statistical learning problem is based on reproducible kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) and kernel sum-of-squares (SoS) methods. First, we extend previous results with a general representer theorem and exhibit the dual formulation of the learning problem. Crucially, such dual formulation can be solved efficiently by accelerated gradient methods with several hundreds or thousands of samples, unlike previous strategies based on off-the-shelf semidefinite programming algorithms. Second, we introduce a new hyperparameter tuning strategy tailored specifically to target adaptivity through bounds on test-conditional coverage. This strategy, based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), is introduced here to tune kernel lengthscales in our framework, but has broader applicability since it could be used in any CP algorithm where the score function is learned. Finally, extensive experiments are conducted to show how our method compares to related work. All figures can be reproduced with the accompanying code at \href{https://www.gitlab.com/drti/ksos-bands}{gitlab.com/drti/ksos-bands}.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025), Dec 2025, San Diego, United States
item.dc:creator: Louis Allain (ENSAI, CREST), S{\'e}bastien da Veiga (ENSAI, CREST, RT-UQ), Brian Staber

item.title: MAGDrop: Momentum Adaptive Gradient Dropout With Provable Generalization Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2510.18410v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Standard dropout applies a fixed, uniform noise rate to all units, ignoring available gradient information. We propose momentum adaptive gradient dropout (MAGDrop), a Bayesian linear layer that adapts per-unit weight noise by tracking an exponential moving average of gradient magnitudes. Units with large recent gradient magnitudes receive less noise to preserve learned features; units with below-average gradient magnitudes receive more noise to promote exploration. This adaptation transforms the classifier head into a data-dependent Bayesian predictor whose mean predictor has no additional inference cost. Our primary contribution is a certificate-aware low-rank posterior, MAGDrop-Subspace, that addresses the tension between strong accuracy and tight bounds from probably approximately correct (PAC)-Bayes theory. A full-head stochastic posterior incurs a Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of approximately 8,625 nats. By confining the posterior to an $r$-dimensional subspace constructed from an independent prior-construction sample $S_0$ and certifying on an independent sample $S$ with $S_0\perp S$, MAGDrop-Subspace reduces KL by approximately a factor of 800 while keeping accuracy close to the baseline. On CIFAR-10 with a 13-layer convolutional neural network and $r=50$, MAGDrop-Subspace achieves a PAC-Bayes Gibbs-risk bound of 0.1882 at 90\% confidence using binary KL inversion, compared with 0.4439 for the full-head baseline. Mean-predictor accuracy is 82.31\%, compared with 83.74\% for the baseline. Complementary accuracy experiments on ImageNet-1K show that MAGDrop reaches top-1 accuracy similar to the strong baseline: 78.57\% compared with 78.51\% on the base Vision Transformer with $16\times16$ patches, and 82.14\% compared with 82.23\% on ConvNeXt-Base.
item.dc:creator: Adeel Safder, Bum Jun Kim

item.title: Scaling Limits of Long-Context Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2605.08505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the long-context limit of softmax self-attention with a fixed query and a random context of $n$ i.i.d. keys on the sphere with the intrinsic dimension of the key distribution held fixed, viewing the inverse temperature $\beta_n$ as the scaling parameter that decides whether attention degenerates into uniform averaging or collapses onto the single closest key. We show that the critical scale at which selectivity emerges is determined by the local exponent of the distance-to-query distribution near zero rather than by global features of the context, and scales like $\beta_n^\ast \asymp n^{2/(d-1)}$ for uniform keys on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Furthermore, we characterize the limiting laws of the ordered attention weights and of the attention output across all regimes of $\beta_n$: a subcritical regime in which the output reduces to a local average around $q$ with explicit deterministic bias and Gaussian fluctuations; a critical regime in which a finite collection of nearest keys retains macroscopic mass without single-key collapse; and a supercritical regime in which all mass concentrates on the closest key. Of notable interest is the subcritical case with identity value matrix where the attention map approximately implements a backward heat equation.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Bruno, Shi Chen, Zhengjiang Lin, Yury Polyanskiy, Philippe Rigollet

item.title: The Symmetric Location Problem: a Song of Efficiency and Robustness
item.description: arXiv:2605.25870v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The aim of this Lecture Note is to introduce the Signal Processing (SP) community to a powerful yet still under-utilised tool: the semiparametric statistics. In short, the semiparametric framework allows us to estimate or perform hypothesis testing on a finite-dimensional parameter $\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^p$ in the presence of an \textit{infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter} $g \in \mathcal{S}$ (i.e. a function), such as the density of the noise. Clearly, this framework is general enough to include almost every SP application. Remarkably, as the title suggests drawing on George R. R. Martin's famous book series, the greatest advantage of semiparametric statistics over parametric and non-parametric ones lies in the fact that it is able to reconcile two seemingly dichotomous concepts: statistical efficiency and distributional robustness. To explain exactly what this means, in this Lecture Note we will focus our attention on the famous and fundamental symmetric location problem.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Fortunati

item.title: How Deep Are Deep GPs, Really? A Sharp Threshold and a Non-Gaussian Limit for Compositional GPs
item.description: arXiv:2606.08218v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compositional priors describe the generic properties of layered functions in deep Bayesian models, where deep neural networks with random weights are a canonical example. In the wide-network limit, the prior is a Gaussian process (GP) with a depth-dependent kernel, and its behaviour as depth grows has been extensively studied through this kernel. Here, we study another case, where each layer itself is a vector valued Gaussian process, and our aim is similarly to understand the limiting behaviour of the prior as depth grows. Previous GP work has established that for the radial basis function (RBF) kernel and a certain range of bandwidths $r$, the prior degenerates in the limit, converging to the set of constant functions, which is not useful as a probabilistic model. In this paper we establish several new results. First, we identify a sharp bandwidth threshold $r_c(d) = \Theta(\sqrt{d})$ above which the limit is degenerate, strengthening the earlier bounds. Second, and more importantly, we show that for $r$ below the threshold $r_c(d)$ the prior converges to a limit distribution $\pi_{\bar{Z}}$. We also prove that these distributions are non-degenerate and non-Gaussian, with non-vanishing dependence between coordinates. In contrast to the previously known degenerate regime, deep Gaussian process priors can therefore admit non-trivial limits. Empirically, we verify the threshold across a range of dimensions $d$, and demonstrate a complex multimodal behaviour of the limit distributions $\pi_{\bar{Z}}$, a regime that becomes increasingly narrow with $d$ and would be hard to identify without knowing the threshold.
item.dc:creator: Mark Kozdoba, Shie Mannor

item.title: Markov Chain CLTs: Resolving Open Problems
item.description: arXiv:2609.07819v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Markov chain central limit theorems (CLTs) and their associated variances are very important for implementing Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms among other applications. H\"aggstr\"om and Rosenthal (2007) presented various results regarding the equality of different formulae for this variance and also posed seven open problems. We resolve all seven in this paper. Our main result is a general characterization of Markov chain CLTs: for stationary and ergodic Markov chains, we prove that the normalized partial sums satisfy a $\sqrt{n}$-CLT if and only if the Poisson equation admits a finite solution with square-integrable martingale differences whose second moment equals the CLT variance. In particular, this result does not require reversibility of the chain or square integrability of the function. It implies that Roberts' holding-probability condition always precludes a $\sqrt{n}$-CLT, and for reversible chains, whenever a $\sqrt{n}$-CLT holds, the variance limit is finite if the function is square-integrable, otherwise undefined. In addition, we develop a general principle that expresses Fourier coefficients as the autocovariances of an ergodic nonreversible Markov chain.
item.dc:creator: Austin Brown, Jeffrey S. Rosenthal, Quan Zhou
